newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Summer sales depress Irish consumer price index.
newsitem.headline: Summer sales depress Irish consumer price index.

text.p: Summer sales were the main factor behind a fall in Irish consumer prices last month, analysts said, adding there was no evidence in the data that weakness of the Irish pound was feeding through to prices.
Figures released on Thursday showed that consumer prices fell 0.1 percent on the month, well below most market forecasts for a 0.2 to 0.3 percent rise.

Analysts attributed the drop to the impact of summer sales and other seasonal factors on clothing and footwear prices, which fell 6.5 percent on the month, and durable household good prices, which were down 0.5 percent.
Oliver Mangan, economist at AIB Group Treasury's bond unit, said the only commodity group to show a rise was food, where prices rose by 0.8 percent on the month.
This was due to higher potato prices, a seasonal factor, which added 0.13 percent to the index, he said.
"They are a very good set of figures," Mangan said, adding that they should lend support to a bond market already buoyed by better-than-expected government borrowings figures.
By 1150 GMT, the benchmark 10-year bond was quoted at 110.75 to yield 6.39 percent and dealers said the spread over the German 10-year had narrowed to 73 basis points from 75 at the opening.
Jim Power, analyst at Bank of Ireland Group Treasury, said prices were being kept down by intense competition in Ireland's retail market.
"We have an extremely competitive retail environment here while if you look at the big picture, internationally we have a benign inflation environment," he said.
But analysts were uncertain whether the punt's 10 percent drop against sterling since the start of the year would yet show up in Irish inflation data.
AIB's Mangan said many companies bought the currency forward at the beginning of the year so it could be September or October before the impact of the drop became apparent.
But NCB's Eunan King said the punt had been falling against sterling since last October and the price effect should have shown up by now.

"Irish purchasers and purchasers in other countries are saying to the UK suppliers, reduce sterling prices or we'll go elsewhere. There is huge downward pressure on the sterling price of UK exports," King added.
